title: AI Chip Design Is Real, but Verification Remains the Top Bottleneck
dek: AI can already write RTL autonomously, but the real bottleneck in the chip pipeline is verification: it eats more than half of development time, and AI can't answer 'what to test.' OpenAI's twenty-person team can shorten the front end, but the back end still needs humans.
why: The author uses firsthand observations and frontline engineers' accounts to rescue 'AI making chips' from clickbait: which are prototypes, which can go into production, and where the real barriers lie.
who: Semiconductor investors, chip company decision-makers, and engineers focused on AI adoption who want to judge whether 'AI chip design' is a real inflection point or fundraising hype.
skip: The opening EDA terminology primer (first minute); those familiar with the chip design flow can skip it.

points.h: K3 has only a front end, no back end
points.body: The raw material for the 'AI 48-hour tapeout' claim is a small inference accelerator called Nano KPU that Kimi unveiled: 238,000 parameters, about 1.46 million standard cells, 0.277MB SRAM, claiming to close timing at 100 MHz within 4 square millimeters and decode at 8,700 tokens/s. But the host looked closely: this RTL went through functional verification only, with no cell placement, routing, physical verification, or sign-off. The so-called 'timing closure' relies on estimates, and 100 MHz is not impressive in an open-source 45nm library—human designers using the same library can achieve 20-450 MHz, and commercial processes can reach 1-3 GHz. K3's goal is not to make a good chip but to prove that an agent can autonomously reach functional completeness.

points.h: AI writing RTL is not news at all
points.body: Many think AI writing chips started with K3, but as early as 2020, NYU researchers used GPT-2 to generate beginner-level RTL, reporting 94.8% accuracy. The defunct eFabless ran AI design contests, and Will Salcedo's GPT-4-generated design actually went to tapeout—one of the earliest known LLM-designed tapeouts. 'AI writing RTL' itself is not new; what has changed is that an agent can run unattended from scratch to functional completeness—autonomy has been distilled.

points.h: The agent's future lies in wrapping toolchains
points.body: While fully autonomous design remains out of reach, the real product form is wrapping LLMs around EDA toolchains: LLMs command deterministic EDA tools via interfaces like MCP or APIs, much like Claude Code lets models call computer tools. Synopsys, Cadence, and Siemens all aim to open their stacks, handing data feedback and control to agents that can run for hours or overnight. Siemens demoed at Semicon Taiwan: an agent dropping hundreds of standard cells one by one into a simulator, measuring load, speed, and power for later design lookup. Re-doing such tedious work for each process node is exactly what you'd hand to AI before leaving work.

points.h: Even the best results keep a human in the loop
points.body: Former xAI engineer Christina Lee's post is the most convincing breakdown the host has seen. Her meta-harness has two layers: an inner layer lets the model call EDA tools to write RTL, synthesize, place and route, and verify; an outer layer lets the model review what went right and wrong in the previous round, propose improvements, and rerun. The first phase only did a MAC multiply-accumulate array, iterating from 900 MHz to 1 GHz; the second phase connected the MAC to SRAM and other modules, and complexity immediately rose. Note that humans keep their hands on the wheel: the so-called goal strings are likely provided by the outer model as reference, but the selection and final sign-off remain with humans. AI is not the boss; it's the co-pilot.

points.h: Jalapeno's real shock is the 20-person team
points.body: OpenAI's Jalapeno demo made many focus on 'RTL to tapeout in just 9 months.' The host reminds us: Synopsys has said elsewhere, without AI, using their tools, it also takes about 9 to 12 months; the chip is not complex, and the starting point is unclear—the architecture concept only began in October 2024. What truly stands out is team size: only 20 to 30 people stood up at the end of the talk. Moreover, this group's token consumption consistently ranks at the top of OpenAI's internal leaderboards, and the RTL was still being changed the day before the freeze. If such a small team can do it, the number of people needed for chip roles could shrink by an order of magnitude—perhaps why they don't emphasize it in the slides.

points.h: Verification is the bottleneck for AI chip design
points.body: The whole industry talks up front-end RTL but glosses over the back end: OpenAI's presentation slides spent much on spec and RTL, while the host guesses the back end was handled by partner Broadcom, thanked only on slide 34; Lee also left the back end to Yosys/OpenLane. The mechanistic asymmetry: PPA (power/performance/area) optimization is a closed loop—generate, verify, measure PPA—AI has a clear reward signal. Verification is not: passing or failing tests does not tell AI how far it is from full coverage, and 'what to test' still relies on humans. Chip bugs cannot be changed once taped out, so seeing a defect on TSMC's silicon on first arrival is the most crushing moment. This explains why verification can consume 50 to 70% of development time, echoing Shibo Chen's line that 'AI designs, humans verify' is the only reassuring approach.

points.h: The biggest threat to front-end wrappers is OpenAI
points.body: Silicon Valley is spawning startups that wrap frontier models with proprietary knowledge to write RTL. The host sees the risk: Anthropic and OpenAI both own models and are making chips; if they decide to open up their chip-specific models, the differentiation of front-end wrappers disappears. So he prefers teams moving toward back end and verification, where end-to-end moats exist. How fast is this field moving? While he was writing, Architect Labs announced that its Redwood chip was fully produced and verified by AI, with specs written only by two architects; even TSMC's 3D IC talk used 'agentic AI.' The host worries his judgment could be overturned by new news within a week or two.

terms.def: Electronic design automation: the software tools needed to design chips, dominated by a few vendors like Synopsys and Cadence.
Register-transfer level: the hardware language layer (Verilog/VHDL) describing data flow and logic—the chip's 'code.'
Process design kit: confidential process parameter packages maintained by foundries and EDA vendors, tightly protected by NDA.
Power, performance, area: the three key metrics for evaluating chip design quality, suitable for closed-loop optimization.
The step of handing the fully verified design data to the foundry to manufacture real chips.
